1d1476560214: The 1955 foreword gives the story of these years in about two pages (pp. xvii–xix):
e38604c0f96e: <0>The book and the name.</0> The book came out in the spring of 1939, and the nameless fellowship "now began to be called Alcoholics Anonymous, from the title of its own book" (p. xvii).
88fc12c73f01: <0>Publicity and the mail.</0> A <1>Liberty</1> magazine article in the fall of 1939 brought 800 inquiries to the small New York office; each was answered, members travelling on business were sent to the prospects, and new groups started (p. xviii). Everyone was surprised to find that "A.A.'s message could be transmitted in the mail as well as by word of mouth" (p. xviii). John D. Rockefeller, Jr.'s dinner for A.A. in 1940 brought more inquiries, and membership reached 2,000 by March 1941 (p. xviii). Then Jack Alexander's <2>Saturday Evening Post</2> article, and "By the close of 1941, A.A. numbered 8,000 members." (p. xviii). "A.A. had become a national institution." (p. xviii).
90815e817a78: <0>Growing pains.</0> The foreword calls what followed an adolescent period. Could so many erratic alcoholics work together? "Would there be quarrels over membership, leadership, and money?" (p. xviii). Those problems came, in every group (p. xix). The conviction grew that "A.A.'s had to hang together or die separately" (p. xix).
00d45211b246: <0>The Traditions.</0> Just as members had found principles to live by, they had to find principles by which groups and A.A. as a whole could survive (p. xix). The foreword lists them in plain words: no alcoholic excluded, leaders who "might serve but never govern" (p. xix), autonomous groups, no professional class, no fees or dues, the least possible organization, attraction rather than promotion, anonymity in the media, and no endorsements, alliances or public controversy (p. xix). It adds that "none of these principles had the force of rules or laws" (p. xix), but by 1950 they were so widely accepted that the first International Conference at Cleveland confirmed them (p. xix).

e61d05cbfd6f: A.A.'s own literature describes A.A. as a fellowship of alcoholics. The 1946 Long Form says A.A.'s membership "ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism" (p. 563). The 1939 Foreword and the later short form of Tradition Three give one requirement, a desire to stop drinking (pp. xiv, 562).
cec3ed634047: An alcoholic with other problems is not shut out. In 1946 Bill W. wrote that if alcohol is an uncontrollable problem to a newcomer and he wants to do something about it, A.A. doesn't care "whether he has other complications or not" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). P-43 (© 1971; this printing updated 2023) names drugs directly: Tradition Three makes no demand that members have no history of drug abuse.
a02fa9beac39: What A.A.'s literature does not claim is to know how to treat drug addiction. In 1957 Bill listed carrying A.A. into "dope addiction" among the early dreams that taught A.A. it could not be all things to all men, and today's group pamphlet calls it "misleading" to suggest that A.A. "knows what to do about drug addiction" (P-16, 2018).
9c0b56fd640d: The 1939 text never speaks to someone whose problem is drugs and not alcohol. The A.A. pamphlet on that subject ("Problems Other Than Alcohol") is not in our sources, so this page doesn't report what it says.
313097ba3eaf: The book is about alcohol. The Foreword to the First Edition gives one requirement for membership, "an honest desire to stop drinking" (p. xiv), and the program chapters are addressed to the alcoholic throughout.
1bfc5f1aaf13: Other drugs come up as part of the drinker's decline. The "real alcoholic" of Chapter 2 starts using "a combination of high-powered sedative and liquor" to get to work, and a doctor may give him "morphine or some sedative with which to taper off" (p. 22). Bill describes drinking "both gin and sedative" (p. 7).
a418f832b08c: Two hospitals in the book treated both. Dr. Silkworth, who wrote "The Doctor's Opinion," directed a hospital "treating alcoholic and drug addiction" (p. xxvii), and Chapter 11 thanks an eastern hospital "for the treatment of alcoholic and drug addiction" (p. 162), whose doctor suggested A.A. to some of his patients. Those passages describe the hospitals. What the doctor writes about, and what Chapter 11 says members went there to do, concerns alcoholics.
7846f4afa678: Nothing in pages 1–164 says what a person addicted only to some other drug should do.
aa0e5248c12d: The 1946 Long Form and Bill's essay
d291040b1108: Tradition Three: "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism." (p. 563). A.A. "may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563).
550a847af5c8: Tradition Five: each group's one primary purpose is carrying its message "to the alcoholic who still suffers" (p. 564).
d7d9ed9920f1: Bill's 1946 essay, which Tradition Three grew out of, is wide open about what else a member may be dealing with. Most early members, he wrote, would have been thrown out under the old membership rules, some "because they had mental as well as alcoholic difficulties" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). His conclusion: if alcohol is an uncontrollable problem to a newcomer and he wants to do something about it, "that is enough for us" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946), whatever other complications he has.
9fb0a7163ec3: <0>1957.</0> In <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> Bill recalls the early fear of the newcomer with "Complications, you know; alcohol mixed with other things" (<2>A.A. Comes of Age</2>, 1957), and how A.A. got over it. In the same book, explaining Traditions Five and Six, he lists the dreams of the early years: hospitals, public education, law reform, and "We would carry A.A. into the dark regions of dope addiction and criminality." (<3>A.A. Comes of Age</3>, 1957). Experience ended those plans: "We of Alcoholics Anonymous could not be all things to all men, and we should not try to be." (<4>A.A. Comes of Age</4>, 1957). He then notes that groups dealing with gambling, delinquency, dope addiction and other problems borrowed from A.A., "but they made their own adaptations" (<5>A.A. Comes of Age</5>, 1957).
0282802563fa: <0>1971 (this printing updated 2023).</0> <1>The Twelve Traditions Illustrated</1> (P-43) says Tradition Three makes no demand that prospective members have no history of drug abuse: "All alcoholics are welcome." (P-43).
f9e42bb2cc7b: <0>2018.</0> <1>The A.A. Group</1> (P-16) says the General Service Conference has recommended that "alcohol and pill" meetings not be listed in A.A. directories. Its reason: "Experience with alcohol is one thing all A.A. members have in common." (P-16, 2018). And: "It is misleading to hint or give the impression that A.A. solves other problems or knows what to do about drug addiction." (P-16, 2018). The same pamphlet says open meetings are available "to anyone interested in Alcoholics Anonymous' program of recovery from alcoholism" (P-16, 2018), with nonalcoholics attending as observers.
7be5279aefc2: Read together, the texts say that A.A. is for alcoholics, that an alcoholic's other problems don't bar him, and that A.A. doesn't claim any special knowledge of drug addiction. They don't directly answer whether a person addicted to some other drug, with no drinking problem, can be an A.A. member. The 1946 essay says a member is a member "as long as he says he is" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946), and that he may join "on the mere suspicion" that he may be an alcoholic (same essay); the Long Form ties membership to alcoholism. The pamphlet that addresses the question head-on, "Problems Other Than Alcohol," is listed in P-16 and P-17 but isn't in our sources.
c49745c329ea: These texts describe what A.A. says about itself. They don't govern other fellowships, which, as Bill wrote in 1957, work their own fields.

1dfb9e74d1ac: Chapter 11, "A Vision for You," written the same year, tells the beginning without dates for Dr. Bob, and dates the third man's recovery: "That was in June, 1935." (p. 158). When the physician sobered for good, "This seemed to prove that one alcoholic could affect another as no nonalcoholic could." (pp. xvi–xvii). 0f23ff00105f: <0>The introduction to Dr. Bob's story</0> (today's edition; it mentions his death in 1950, so it was written after then): "The birth of our Society dates from his first day of permanent sobriety, June 10, 1935." (p. 171).
29ccdf8c9c39: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948</0> (his last major talk, in P-53) gave the same date for his last drink, "and that was on the 10th of June, 1935" (P-53).
bdefbc587722: <0>A.A. Comes of Age (1957).</0> The book opens with the 1955 St. Louis convention, held to commemorate "the twentieth anniversary of its founding" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). c82fe51b827f: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (1980):</0> "Although arguments have been and will be made for other significant occasions in A.A. history, it is generally agreed that Alcoholics Anonymous began there, in Akron, on that date: June 10, 1935." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).
4a9a480d410c: <0>Pass It On (1984)</0> calls it the date "now honored as the date when A.A. really began" (Pass It On, 1984).
e66ea97bd50f: <0>The meeting.</0> Bill and Dr. Bob met on a Sunday in May 1935, Mother's Day (p. 179; A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). 9bae811a29ce: The 1939 text doesn't prescribe a meeting format. It describes the early gatherings in the "western city" of Chapter 11, Akron: informal evenings in members' homes, and one night a week set apart as "a time and place where new people might bring their problems" (p. 160), where a newcomer heard the story of someone "whose experience closely tallied with his own" (p. 160).
f99f1f3ffa11: Today's group pamphlet describes the common kinds of meeting (discussion, speaker, beginners, Step, Tradition or Big Book) and says "No one type or format is the best for an A.A. meeting" (P-16, 2018). Each group decides its own format.
54a33e690ba0: Customs differ from place to place. P-43 says the local group "is free to work out its own customs" (P-43).
ebd656cddfc7: What every description shares is alcoholics talking with alcoholics about their own experience.
c06b3aee93e9: Chapter 11, "A Vision for You," gives the only account of meetings in the first 164 pages (pp. 159–162): - <0>Most evenings, informally.</0> "Scarce an evening passed that someone's home did not shelter a little gathering of men and women, happy in their release, and constantly thinking how they might present their discovery to some newcomer." (p. 159). - <1>One night a week.</1> It became customary to "set apart one night a week for a meeting" (p. 159) for "anyone or everyone interested in a spiritual way of life" (p. 160). Aside from fellowship and sociability, "the prime object was to provide a time and place where new people might bring their problems" (p. 160). - <2>What a newcomer found.</2> A man still dazed from the hospital heard, "in an upper room of this house," the story of a man whose experience matched his own (p. 160). The book names what reached him: "The very practical approach to his problems, the absence of intolerance of any kind, the informality, the genuine democracy, the uncanny understanding which these people had were irresistible." (p. 160). - <3>Size.</3> By 1939 the house could hardly hold its weekly visitors, "sixty or eighty as a rule" (p. 161). - <4>More than meetings.</4> "But life among Alcoholics Anonymous is more than attending gatherings and visiting hospitals." (p. 161). Members cleaned up old scrapes, settled family differences, and lent money and found jobs for each other "when justified" (p. 161). - <5>In the East</5>, there were "informal meetings such as we have described to you" (p. 162).
0eeaa0c29b14: Elsewhere the program chapters say nothing about how a meeting runs: no readings, no order of business, no way of introducing yourself. The nearest it comes is its description of its own stories, which disclose "what we used to be like, what happened, and what we are like now" (p. 58).
8d0be09ec54e: "When A.A. was very young we met in homes." (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947). People came miles for the meeting and stayed for hours afterward "at coffee, cake, and eager, intimate talk" (same essay). When homes became too small, New York moved to a tailor's workshop, a rented room at Steinway Hall, and then a club.
9de635ea90f8: Members dropped money in "the hat" to pay the rent (P-17, "Money", 1946).
d5f2edf9a6d5: In 1946 groups ran from near-secret meetings for alcoholics only to public meetings with speakers on the platform (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). See <0>What's the difference between open and closed meetings? Can family or friends come?</0>

Group</0> (P-16) describes what is common, not what is required: - <1>Kinds of meeting:</1> discussion (a chair picks a topic), speaker (members tell "what they were like, what happened and what they are like now," as the pamphlet puts it, after the Big Book), beginners (often questions and answers, or Steps One to Three), and Step, Tradition or Big Book study; also business, group inventory and service meetings. - <2>Usual procedure:</2> the chair "usually opens the meeting with the A.A. Preamble and a few remarks" (P-16, 2018). Some groups have a moment of silence or the Serenity Prayer, or a reading from the Big Book, often from Chapter 5 or Chapter 3. Many close with a moment of silence and a prayer, or the Responsibility Declaration. A basket may be passed for contributions. - <3>Who decides:</3> meetings, open or closed, are "conducted by A.A. members who determine the format of their meetings" (P-16, 2018). - <4>Before and after:</4> coffee and conversation, and members helping set up and clean up.
ac163d3d287c: The Foreword to the Fourth Edition (2001) adds that members with computers "can participate in meetings online" (p. xxiv).
30f675b90d7a: There is no single A.A. meeting. The 1939 text shows the purpose (a place where newcomers bring their problems and hear from people who have recovered), and the later pamphlets show that groups have built many formats around it, each group choosing its own. She had: a once well-known lawyer who had just beaten up a couple of nurses, had been in eight times in six months, and was strapped down (p. 156). One of them answered, "Put him in a private room." (p. 157).
6b43da8053fd: That is Chapter 7's method in action: ask the hospitals for a drinker who wants help, and go to him (see <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>).

He doubted it: he had prayed on hangover mornings and been drunk again by nine (p. 158). On the third day he gave his life to the care and direction of his Creator, and that afternoon he walked out "a free man" (p. 158). "That was in June, 1935. He never drank again." (p. 158). a695941f310e: Today's group pamphlet lists what A.A. does not do: no hospitalization, drugs or treatment; no housing, food, clothing, jobs or money; no domestic or vocational counseling (P-16, 2018).

(p. 91). An approach through a doctor or an institution "is a better bet" than through his family (p. 91). Chapter 11 lists "lending money and securing jobs for each other, when justified" among everyday events (p. 161). - <2>The limit.</2> The man who expects you "to act only as a banker for his financial difficulties or a nurse for his sprees" may have to be dropped until he changes his mind (p. 95). 2a4d744dda72: The next sentence moves the reader on: "Being convinced, we were at Step Three" (p. 60).
a332300dc480: Two small words carry weight: "probably" in (b) and "if He were sought" in (c). The book hedges and states a condition, and both match what it said in the earlier chapters.

0faa208b4936: Then come the a, b, c, introduced as ideas the book has already made clear, not as new rules. Being convinced of them, "we were at Step Three" (p. 60). The book goes straight into what Step Three means, starting with "The first requirement is that we be convinced that any life run on self-will can hardly be a success." (p. 60)
d4cba8c664ef: The three ideas cover the ground of Steps One and Two: (a) is close to Step One's wording, "our lives had become unmanageable" (p. 59), and (b) and (c) to Step Two's "a Power greater than ourselves could restore us to sanity" (p. 59). The book doesn't label them that way. What it says is that being convinced of them puts the reader at Step Three.
349a06429bb0: The book names its sources for them: the description of the alcoholic (Chapters 2–3), the chapter to the agnostic (Chapter 4), and the members' stories.
f1deb9e3436f: <0>(a) We were alcoholic and couldn't manage our own lives.</0> Chapter 3: "We alcoholics are men and women who have lost the ability to control our drinking." (p. 30) Chapter 2: "We are without defense against the first drink." (p. 24)
e66bc5178bf8: <0>(b) Probably no human power could have relieved our alcoholism.</0> The word "probably" fits the earlier chapters, which keep leaving a little room: - Chapter 3 says the alcoholic has no effective defense against the first drink, and "Except in a few rare cases, neither he nor any other human being can provide such a defense." (p. 43) - Whether a person can quit "upon a nonspiritual basis," it says, depends on how far he has already lost the power to choose (p. 34). - If anyone showing loss of control can turn around and "drink like a gentleman, our hats are off to him" (p. 31). - A doctor quoted on p. 43 says that two of the members "were 100% hopeless, apart from divine help" (p. 43).
9ce695d0bb0d: <0>(c) God could and would if He were sought.</0> Chapter 4 sets the condition low. The reader needs only to ask "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (p. 47) "We found that God does not make too hard terms with those who seek Him." (p. 46) And the God sought is the reader's own conception: "When, therefore, we speak to you of God, we mean your own conception of God." (p. 47)

3a47de41aa4b: How were Akron and New York different in the early years?
c53d2140ae14: Akron was A.A.'s first group, formed in 1935 around Dr. Bob, and for its first years it was the larger and more successful of the two. New York, around Bill W., took shape more slowly; for a long time the people he took into his Brooklyn home stayed drunk.
051b9d98ef15: New York's alcoholics left the Oxford Group in 1937. Akron's stayed inside it, meeting at the home of T. Henry and Clarace Williams, until late 1939. It had its own ways, hospitalizing prospects and having them make a formal "surrender" on their knees, and it kept the Oxford Group's morning quiet time, Bible reading and "absolutes."
7e66ca3efadf: When the Big Book was written, Bill said Akron gave him "the warmest support" while New York gave the drafts "a real mauling," and the two groups favored different titles. A later history adds that Akron had its own quarrels over the book.
a7b1aa047607: The 1939 Big Book itself says the same thing was happening in the East "under only slightly different conditions." The sources treat it as one fellowship with two centers.
9b69c1ccea17: Chapter 11, "A Vision for You," describes the "western city" (Akron) without naming it. After the first three, "A year and six months later these three had succeeded with seven more." (p. 159). A weekly meeting began, open to anyone interested in a spiritual way of life (pp. 159–160), and a couple "placed their large home at the disposal of this strangely assorted crowd" (p. 160). By 1939 that house drew sixty or eighty a week, and a community thirty miles away had fifteen members (p. 161).
607f9718609e: Then: "Under only slightly different conditions, the same thing is taking place in many eastern cities." (p. 161). In one of them was a hospital where a doctor sent them patients, and there were informal meetings "where you may now see scores of members" (p. 162). "There is a good bit of travel between East and West and we foresee a great increase in this helpful interchange." (p. 162).
6994e30c56a3: The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition gives the order: the first group formed at Akron in the summer of 1935, "though no one realized it at the time" (p. xvii); "A second small group promptly took shape at New York" (p. xvii), followed by Cleveland.
374c0b8ddc24: New York's slow start (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)
830bed71133a: Bill had no success in New York until he came home from Akron in September 1935 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He and Lois filled their Clinton Street house with alcoholics and, he says, did not sober up a single one, though "we did pick up a lot of knowledge" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The first to recover were Henry P. and Fitz M. (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Meanwhile, "Out in Akron, in the houses of Dr. Bob and Wally, the home-sobering treatment fared better." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <0>How did A.A. grow from two people?</0>
b2fc537f1924: The New Yorkers parted from the Oxford Groups in the latter part of 1937 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In Akron the alcoholics went on meeting with Oxford Groupers at the Williamses' house until "well after the A.A. book was published" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Writing of the fall of 1938, Bill says that "In important matters there was still considerable disagreement" between the Eastern and Midwestern viewpoints (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957): Akron still talked of the four absolutes, which New York had dropped (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <0>What did early A.A. take from the Oxford Group, and why did it separate?</0>
19ac5d7741a9: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980) describes the Akron practice. Prospects were hospitalized for five to eight days (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980) and had to make a "surrender," kneeling and praying in front of other members; one member recalled that "You couldn't go to a meeting until you did it." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Morning quiet time and spiritual reading were emphasized (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). Akron members also told less of their drinking histories at meetings; one recalled that "Bill was in favor of having an A.A. member qualify or tell how he became an alcoholic" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).
7deaf5ace7b4: <0>The 1937 plan.</0> When Bill and Dr. Bob put the idea of a book, hospitals and paid missionaries to eighteen Akron members, the members "really did work us over," and it passed by the barest majority (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Back home, "Our little New York group gave me more encouragement than had the Akronites." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
bb68513b5b0f: <0>The chapters.</0> Drafts went to Dr. Bob in Akron, "where we had nothing but the warmest support," while in New York the chapters "got a real mauling" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Akronites liked the new Steps; in New York the debate "was doubled and redoubled" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
32534babfafa: <0>The stories.</0> Akron, the larger group with more case histories, produced eighteen stories with the help of a former newspaperman, Jim S.; New York produced ten, written by the members themselves (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
0656be03602c: <0>The title.</0> New York leaned to "Alcoholics Anonymous"; in Akron a considerable majority favored "The Way Out" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). See <1>How did Alcoholics Anonymous get its name? Was "The Way Out" the title?</1>
b59767f9af4e: <0>Akron and the book.</0> Bill (1957) recalls only warm support from Akron (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> (1980) says some Akron members "wanted no part of the book" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), quotes Dorothy S. M.: "For a time, we thought the whole Akron group might break up over the book." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and comments that Bill "might have been assuming that his part of the stove was warmer." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).
209360692eb8: <0>Why New York argued more.</0> <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) suggests Akron members may have been more attuned to Bill's spiritual ideas and Dr. Bob's influence carried them, while New York had more agnostics and skeptics (Pass It On, 1984). That is the 1984 authors' guess; the earlier texts don't give a reason.
f3ecb42fb608: <0>The meditation.</0> Bill later wondered why Wally and Annabelle G. sobered up so many in their Akron home while he and Lois sobered none in theirs. He wasn't sure: "Maybe they just hit the right cases." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). But he also said, "I sort of always felt that something was lost from A.A. when we stopped emphasizing the morning meditation." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). The same book adds that "it was all one Fellowship" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980).

bd34e2495ba7: What does the Big Book mean by alcoholism as an illness?
1b78b6dc429f: The Big Book calls alcoholism an "illness" and a "malady": "we have come to believe it an illness" (p. 18). It is an illness of body and mind together, it gets worse over time, and it is never cured (pp. xxvi, 22–24, 30, 85).
bf54c1666c85: The book places the heart of the problem in the mind, the alcoholic's lack of defense against the first drink (pp. 23–24), and beneath that in the spirit. Its answer is a spiritual one: "an illness which only a spiritual experience will conquer" (p. 44).
942c148ebc5d: The main text uses "illness," not "disease." In the first 164 pages "disease" appears once, as "spiritual disease," about resentment (p. 64). Calling alcoholism "a disease" comes in the personal stories (pp. 187, 416).
1a200e9cd6b8: Calling it an illness doesn't excuse anything in the book. The same pages say our troubles are "of our own making" (pp. 62, 103), and the illness is the reason to act, not a reason not to.
c0b58b8c319c: Across the forewords, Chapters 1–11 and the appendices, the book's word is <0>illness</0> (Chapters 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 10) or <1>malady</1> (Chapters 2, 5, 7, 10), and it often calls the alcoholic a <2>sick</2> man. The word <3>disease</3> appears once in those pages: "From it stem all forms of spiritual disease, for we have been not only mentally and physically ill, we have been spiritually sick" (p. 64). "It" there is resentment, not alcoholism.
f4ae69c69258: "Disease" for alcoholism does appear in the personal stories. In "Alcoholic Anonymous Number Three" (Part I), Bill W. and Dr. Bob tell the man in the bed, "No, you have a disease" (p. 187), and Bill speaks of being cured "of this terrible disease" (p. 191). That story dates itself to about 1954 ("Nineteen years ago last summer," p. 188). In "Acceptance Was the Answer" (Part II), a member writes that it helped him to see "alcoholism was a disease, not a moral issue" (p. 416). These are members' own words in the stories, not the program text.
035920877655: The first voice in the book is a doctor's. Dr. Silkworth's theory is that alcohol works on these drinkers like an allergy, setting off a craving that "never occurs in the average temperate drinker" (p. xxviii). The A.A. members who introduce him agree that "the body of the alcoholic is quite as abnormal as his mind" and add that "our bodies were sickened as well" (p. xxvi). They're careful about the theory itself: "As laymen, our opinion as to its soundness may, of course, mean little" (p. xxvi).
f6b39c6d67c9: Chapter 2 says the same from experience. Once the alcoholic takes any alcohol at all, "something happens, both in the bodily and mental sense" that makes it almost impossible to stop (pp. 22–23). Chapter 7 tells the helper to talk about "the conditions of body and mind which accompany it" (p. 92).
f091af09aad3: But the book is clear about where the real trouble lies. Since the illness can't start unless the alcoholic takes the first drink, "the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body" (p. 23). Most alcoholics "have lost the power of choice in drink" (p. 24). "We are without defense against the first drink" (p. 24). There is "the obsession that somehow, someday, they will beat the game" (p. 23). Chapter 3 shows that mental blank spot at length, in Jim, the jay-walker and Fred (pp. 35–43).
3504619f3088: It's also an illness that gets worse and doesn't go away. Chapter 3 calls it a progressive illness in which we get worse, never better, and compares alcoholics to men who have lost their legs and never grow new ones (p. 30). "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic" (p. 33). Even after recovery, "We are not cured of alcoholism" (p. 85).
84c29af193dd: The book goes one level deeper. Resentment is the chief offender, and "When the spiritual malady is overcome, we straighten out mentally and physically" (p. 64). Drinking itself "was but a symptom" (p. 64). The root, the book says, is "Selfishness—self-centeredness!" (p. 62). That's why the illness can only be met by a spiritual experience (p. 44) and why Dr. Silkworth says recovery requires "an entire psychic change" (p. xxix).
c81a2279572f: How the book uses the idea
fd7d547d4e8c: The illness idea runs through the book's practical advice: - <0>To the newcomer:</0> the helper should tell him how "you finally learned that you were sick" and "Continue to speak of alcoholism as an illness, a fatal malady" (p. 92). You can be frank about how hopeless the illness is because you have a solution to offer, and the more hopeless he feels, the more likely he is to take your suggestions (pp. 92, 94). - <1>To families:</1> wives are reminded that "alcoholism is an illness over which we could not possibly have had any power" (p. 118). They're told to treat the man as a sick person (p. 100) and to tell friends "the nature of his illness" (p. 115). - <2>To employers:</2> "explain alcoholism, the illness" (p. 142), and treat the man as gravely ill. - <3>In resentment:</3> the people who wronged us were "perhaps spiritually sick" too (p. 66), to be treated as a sick friend (p. 67).
dd25c905e7ca: The illness doesn't take away responsibility. The book that calls alcoholism an illness also says our troubles "are basically of our own making" (p. 62), and Chapter 7 ends: "After all, our problems were of our own making" (p. 103). The illness explains why willpower failed. It's the reason the program asks for so much action (pp. 58–103), not a reason to wait.
86f26f15f443: And the book doesn't claim to settle the medical question. On why the alcoholic reacts as he does, "Perhaps there never will be a full answer to these questions" (p. 22).

3b8c880f5e10: Its plainest test is in Chapter 4: "If, when you honestly want to, you find you cannot quit entirely, or if when drinking, you have little control over the amount you take, you are probably alcoholic." (p. 44).
2c037b1baa41: It describes three kinds of drinker, the moderate drinker, the hard drinker and the "real alcoholic," and the mark of the last is losing control once he starts (pp. 20–21). It also suggests two experiments: try some controlled drinking (pp. 31–32), or try leaving liquor alone for a year (p. 34).
20576155789b: A.A. itself doesn't diagnose anyone. Today's group pamphlet says A.A. does not "Make medical or psychological diagnoses or prognoses" (P-16, 2018).
b8162412a3c8: Chapter 2 sorts drinkers this way (pp. 20–22): - <0>The moderate drinker</0> has "little trouble in giving up liquor entirely if they have good reason for it" (p. 20); he can take it or leave it alone. - <1>The hard drinker</1> may harm his health, but given a strong enough reason, such as ill health, falling in love or a doctor's warning, he "can also stop or moderate, although he may find it difficult and troublesome and may even need medical attention" (p. 21). - <2>The real alcoholic</2> "may start off as a moderate drinker" but "at some stage of his drinking career he begins to lose all control of his liquor consumption, once he starts to drink" (p. 21). The chapter describes him for a page and a half, then adds that this "is by no means a comprehensive picture of the true alcoholic" (p. 22).
cd2236ac2f95: The chapter's center is the first drink. Once the alcoholic takes any alcohol, something happens "both in the bodily and mental sense" that makes it virtually impossible for him to stop (pp. 22–23); and at certain times "We are without defense against the first drink." (p. 24).
f6eef843876e: Chapter 3 is about who is and isn't "one of us": - <0>The first admission is inside.</0> "We learned that we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics." (p. 30). - <1>The methods that didn't work</1> are listed at length: beer only, limiting the number of drinks, never drinking alone, never in the morning, switching drinks, swearing off, and more (p. 31). - <2>The barroom test.</2> "Step over to the nearest barroom and try some controlled drinking." (p. 31). Try to drink and stop abruptly, more than once. "It will not take long for you to decide, if you are honest with yourself about it." (p. 32). - <3>The year test.</3> "If anyone questions whether he has entered this dangerous area, let him try leaving liquor alone for one year." (p. 34). If he is a real alcoholic and far advanced, there is "scant chance of success" (p. 34). But passing the test doesn't settle it either: "Though you may be able to stop for a considerable period, you may yet be a potential alcoholic." (p. 34). - <4>Length and amount aren't the measure.</4> "To be gravely affected, one does not necessarily have to drink a long time nor take the quantities some of us have." (p. 33). Several early members of thirty or less had been drinking only a few years and found themselves "as helpless as those who had been drinking twenty years" (p. 33). - <5>Why it's hard to see.</5> Most members had been unwilling to admit they were real alcoholics: "No person likes to think he is bodily and mentally different from his fellows." (p. 30). The obsession that "somehow, someday he will control and enjoy his drinking" (p. 30) is the great obsession of every abnormal drinker.
2c5aca9545da: The chapter states its own aim: to help readers "determine, to their own satisfaction, whether they are one of us" (p. 34).
aac5e97302f2: In "The Doctor's Opinion," Dr. Silkworth names one thing all his types of alcoholic have in common: "they cannot start drinking without developing the phenomenon of craving" (p. xxx). He also describes the restlessness, irritability and discontent of the alcoholic who can't feel at ease without a drink (pp. xxviii–xxix).

A member talking with a prospect should "be careful not to brand him as an alcoholic" (p. 92), and let him draw his own conclusion. Bill W.'s 1946 essay on membership says a newcomer can join A.A. 3d47426a0bbc: The phrase appears three times in the Big Book's main text, each time tied to the Steps. It's on p. 58, just before the Steps are listed, and twice in the pages on amends: p. 76, opening Steps Eight and Nine, and p. 79.
eb12a07796ac: On p. 58 it's something the reader decides for himself: "If you have decided you want what we have and are willing to go to any length to get it—then you are ready to take certain steps." (p. 58)
7ba292ad2e70: In the amends pages it means accepting what it costs <0>us</0>: "We may lose our position or reputation or face jail, but we are willing." (p. 79)
4714b236cff7: The very next paragraph limits it where other people would pay: we "are not to be the hasty and foolish martyr who would needlessly sacrifice others to save himself" (p. 79). Read in place, "any length" is about what we'll bear ourselves, not about what we may do to others.
4e72af2c9f2d: <0>1. Before the Steps (p. 58).</0> The sentence opens with a decision the reader makes: "If you have decided you want what we have" (p. 58). Being willing to go to any length is what makes him "ready to take certain steps" (p. 58). The next paragraph says how the writers met that willingness: "At some of these we balked." (p. 58) They looked for an easier, softer way and "could not" find one (p. 58).
d55119a37403: <0>2. Starting the amends (p. 76).</0> After Steps Six and Seven, the book turns to Steps Eight and Nine: "Now we go out to our fellows and repair the damage done in the past." (p. 76) If we lack the will to do it, "we ask until it comes" (p. 76). Then it looks back to p. 58: "Remember it was agreed at the beginning we would go to any lengths for victory over alcohol." (p. 76)
32c55640a5ec: <0>3. The hard amends (p. 79).</0> For amends that could cost a job or bring legal trouble, the book reminds the reader "that we have decided to go to any lengths to find a spiritual experience" (p. 79). We ask for strength to do the right thing "no matter what the personal consequences may be" (p. 79). "We must not shrink at anything." (p. 79)

628e0493092b: <0>The usual advice, listed and rejected.</0> People had said we must not go where liquor is served, must shun friends who drink, must avoid films with drinking scenes, must not go into bars (pp. 100–101). 6fcb670e00c6: <0>The motive.</0> "Be sure you are on solid spiritual ground before you start and that your motive in going is thoroughly good" (p. 102). "Do not think of what you will get out of the occasion. Think of what you can bring to it" (p. 102).

a6c85de895a0: "Bedevilments" is on page 52 of the Big Book, in Chapter 4, "We Agnostics." It's the book's word for a list of eight troubles the writers had with living (p. 52).
903d1b8155a5: The list, in the book's order: trouble with personal relationships; couldn't control our emotional natures; a prey to misery and depression; couldn't make a living; a feeling of uselessness; full of fear; unhappy; couldn't seem to be of real help to other people (p. 52).
b9a6c6e503d0: Drinking isn't on the list. A page earlier the book says the members' stories, "Leaving aside the drink question," tell why living was so unsatisfactory (p. 51).
e698c29fb5d3: In its place the list is part of an argument to the agnostic reader: the modern age drops ideas that don't work for ones that do, so why not do the same with these problems? The answer follows: "Our ideas did not work. But the God idea did." (p. 52) The context confirms what the list says and shows what it's there for.
2307f968697f: Pages 51–53 make one argument, in steps: 1. <0>The world changes its mind when the evidence is in.</0> Material progress in the last century came from the spirit of scientific inquiry (p. 51). People once thought a round earth preposterous; newspapers were afraid to print the Wright brothers' flight; thirty years later air travel was ordinary (pp. 51–52). 2. <1>Are we doing the opposite about the spirit?</1> "Are not some of us just as biased and unreasonable about the realm of the spirit as were the ancients about the realm of the material?" (p. 51) The age is marked by the readiness to "throw away the theory or gadget which does not work for something new which does" (p. 52). 3. <2>Then apply that to our own lives.</2> "We had to ask ourselves why we shouldn't apply to our human problems this same readiness to change our point of view." (p. 52) 4. <3>The list.</3> The eight troubles above, ending with a question: wasn't "a basic solution of these bedevilments more important than whether we should see newsreels of lunar flight? Of course it was." (p. 52) 5. <4>What they saw work.</4> "When we saw others solve their problems by a simple reliance upon the Spirit of the Universe, we had to stop doubting the power of God." (p. 52) They had been relying on self-sufficiency; when others showed them that "God-sufficiency" worked, they felt like the people who had said the Wrights would never fly (pp. 52–53).
7a7a215fddeb: A few things the text shows: - <0>It's "we."</0> The list is the writers describing themselves: "We were having trouble with personal relationships" (p. 52). The book doesn't present it here as a test for the reader or name it a symptom of anything. - <1>It's about living, not drinking.</1> The book sets drink aside on purpose in this stretch (p. 51). The list is what was wrong with life itself. - <2>It ends with other people.</2> The last item is that "we couldn't seem to be of real help to other people" (p. 52). The book's chapter on Step Twelve later says "To be helpful is our only aim" (p. 89). - <3>It's offered as a reason, not a verdict.</3> The chapter is trying to persuade agnostic readers, as the writers once were, to give the spiritual side of life the fair hearing the writers admit they never gave it (p. 50). It says plainly it is arguing: "we are at pains to tell why we think our present faith is reasonable" (p. 53).

cf201f30f984: Where the text agrees with the saying
2a88d56283b8: The Big Book does say, more than once, that the alcoholic's own mind couldn't get him sober:
60a344730109: <0>Reason lost to the first drink.</0> "Our sound reasoning failed to hold us in check. The insane idea won out." (p. 37).
bacc8a4f5444: <0>Self-knowledge failed.</0> After treatment Bill thought "Surely this was the answer—self-knowledge." (p. 7), and then drank again (p. 7). Fred, after his relapse, "saw that will power and self-knowledge would not help in those strange mental blank spots" (p. 42). The chapter says the real alcoholic "will be absolutely unable to stop drinking on the basis of self-knowledge" (p. 39).
2b234e43382e: <0>Their own ideas.</0> "Our ideas did not work. But the God idea did." (p. 52). Earlier the same chapter admits that "we agnostics and atheists chose to believe that our human intelligence was the last word" (p. 49).
c486df2e7111: <0>Self-will.</0> The alcoholic is "an extreme example of self-will run riot" (p. 62), and "our troubles, we think, are basically of our own making" (p. 62).
728261346ff0: <0>Reason has limits.</0> "Hence, we saw that reason isn't everything." (p. 54). Reason as most of us use it isn't entirely dependable, "though it emanate from our best minds" (pp. 54–55). The "best minds" there are the experts who once proved men could never fly (p. 55), not the alcoholic in particular.
d8b5dedd64c8: Where the text disagrees with how the saying is often used
a93cc8da5ec6: When the saying is used to mean "don't trust your mind, don't think, just do what you're told," the program text says otherwise:
f29b7725300e: <0>Reason is a gift.</0> "Logic is great stuff. We liked it. We still like it." (p. 53). "It is not by chance we were given the power to reason" (p. 53). The writers say they wouldn't be satisfied with a proposal that didn't lend itself to reasonable approach (p. 53), and they spend Chapter 4 giving reasons (pp. 48–55).
90b48717e7b0: <0>Thinking, cleaned up, is used every day.</0> Step Eleven's morning: ask God to direct our thinking, "especially asking that it be divorced from self-pity, dishonest or self-seeking motives" (p. 86). "Under these conditions we can employ our mental faculties with assurance, for after all God gave us brains to use." (p. 86). "Our thought-life will be placed on a much higher plane when our thinking is cleared of wrong motives." (p. 86).
0cd2a04003ec: <0>Bill's way of checking his thinking.</0> "I was to test my thinking by the new God-consciousness within." (p. 13).
c6f32154fe54: <0>Where the thinking goes wrong.</0> Apart from self-will (above), the book locates the trouble in drink: the alcoholic "is often perfectly sensible and well balanced concerning everything except liquor" (p. 21). "However intelligent we may have been in other respects, where alcohol has been involved, we have been strangely insane." (p. 38). Chapter 10 calls him "a victim of crooked thinking, directly caused by the action of alcohol on his brain" (p. 140).
85d7e9bae966: The saying holds a real point from the book: the alcoholic's own reasoning, will power and self-knowledge didn't stop him drinking, and self-will got him into trouble. The book doesn't conclude that thinking is the enemy. It says the mind fails on the subject of the first drink and when it is run by selfish motives, and that the answer is a Power greater than ourselves, after which the reader is told to use his brains with assurance (p. 86). See: <0>Is "it's not a drinking problem, it's a thinking problem" in the Big Book?</0>

7f5ec4a31f9b: Yes. Bill W. wrote the chapters through 1938, reading them to the New York group and sending them to Dr. Bob in Akron for comment. The first two chapters were copied in mid-1938 to use in a fund-raising prospectus.

3fb8f5ae7e5c: There have been four editions: 1939, 1955, 1976 and 2001 (p. xi). In all of them the first part of the book, "describing the A.A. recovery program, has been left largely untouched" (p. xi), and "The Doctor's Opinion" has been kept intact (p. xi).
8278ffaf57ca: The chief change each time was in the personal stories: stories were added, edited and dropped so the book would "represent the current membership" (p. xii) and reach more alcoholics.
aea4423fb4e0: The 1955 edition also added the appendices, the Twelve Traditions and directions for contacting A.A. (p. xi). The 2001 edition added the Twelve Concepts (p. xii). Each edition added its own foreword.
cedfe0755296: "Largely" is the honest word. Footnotes have been added to the 1939 chapters, and small details in the text follow the edition, such as the number of stories on p. 29. Our sources have only the fourth edition, so it can't show a line-by-line comparison with 1939.
f057ccd9cdcc: The Preface to the fourth edition explains why: because the book has become "the basic text for our Society" and helped so many recover, "there exists strong sentiment against any radical changes being made in it" (p. xi). So the program chapters were left largely untouched in the 1955, 1976 and 2001 revisions, and "The Doctor's Opinion" was "kept intact, just as it was originally written in 1939" (p. xi). The Foreword to the First Edition is reprinted "as it appeared in the first printing of the first edition in 1939" (p. xiii).
f198f28f3eec: Later accounts put it more strongly. Bill W., announcing the second edition at the 1955 convention, said "the old familiar text of the book stands unchanged" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says the original text of the first 11 chapters was unchanged in 1955 (Pass It On, 1984). <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> (2003) says the first 164 pages "have remained largely unchanged" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). The Preface's "largely" is the more careful word, and the text bears it out (see below).
e1df651658fd: <0>First edition, April 1939</0> (p. xi). Sixteen printings, 1939 to 1955 (p. iv). More than 300,000 copies circulated (p. xi). It even changed between printings: - The title page first described "More Than One Hundred Men," changed by the second printing to "Thousands of Men and Women" (Pass It On, 1984). - One story, "Lone Endeavor," "appeared only in first printing of first edition" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). - Bill (1969) recalled that an early printing "expressed great concern lest we be flooded with more people than we could take care of" (P-53), out of fear that "so-called undesirable people" (P-53) might come, and said "that part of the book was eliminated after the first printing" (P-53). P-53's footnote points to the first-edition foreword's worry about "the overwhelming number of personal appeals" (P-53), a line today's reprint of that foreword still carries (p. xiii); our sources can't show which passage Bill had in mind. - Appendix II, "Spiritual Experience," says "our first printing gave many readers the impression" (p. 567) that the personality change had to be sudden and spectacular, and corrects it, so it was written after the first printing; the Preface says the appendices entered the book with the second edition (p. xi). Our sources don't say exactly when Appendix II was written.
dbe733226784: <0>Second edition, 1955</0> (p. xi). More than 1,150,500 copies (p. xi). It added "the appendices, the Twelve Traditions, and the directions for getting in touch with A.A." (p. xi), and a new foreword describing the fellowship "as it was in 1955" (p. xv). The story section was rebuilt and divided into three parts, "Pioneers of A.A.," "They Stopped in Time" and "They Lost Nearly All" (pp. xi–xii). Bill's story, Dr. Bob's and one other were kept intact; three were edited (one retitled); two were rewritten under new titles; thirty new stories were added (pp. xi–xii). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) adds that Bill made a point of including the story of A.A. number three, Bill D., who hadn't written one for 1939 (Pass It On, 1984). <2>Experience, Strength and Hope</2> (2003) quotes Bill's 1954 guidance: the audience "is people who are coming to Alcoholics Anonymous now" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003).
f4866667ef1d: <0>Third edition, 1976</0> (p. xi). About 19,550,000 copies in all formats (p. xi). Part I was left unchanged; Part II kept nine stories and added eight; Part III kept eight and added five (p. xii). A new foreword reported more than a million members in over 90 countries (p. xxii).
2ea3d9604639: <0>Fourth edition, 2001.</0> It added the Twelve Concepts for World Service (p. xii), now Appendix VII (p. 574), and a new foreword (p. xxiii). In the stories, Part I gained one new story and two moved from Part III, and lost six; Part II kept six, added eleven and dropped eleven; Part III added twelve and dropped eight, besides the two moved (p. xii). The book now has forty-two stories (p. xii). <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> (2003) says the 1997 General Service Conference asked for the edition, that more than 1,200 manuscripts came in, and that the changes "were the most extensive yet" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). The new stories, the fourth-edition foreword says, represent a membership whose "characteristics—of age, gender, race, and culture—have widened and have deepened" (p. xxiii).
f3951c2ecc0a: The fourth edition shows its own seams: - <0>Footnotes.</0> Several notes carry later dates: membership figures for 2006 and 2007 (pp. 16, 162) and a 2003 survey of members' ages (p. 34). Others were plainly written later: a note on Al-Anon, formed "about thirteen years after this chapter was written" (p. 121), and one identifying Bill and Dr. Bob, who "later became co-founders of A.A." (p. 155). Chapter 8 now carries a note that it was "Written in 1939, when there were few women in A.A." (p. 104). Our copy is the thirty-second printing, December 2013 (p. iv), and the fourth-edition foreword has a note dated 2013 (p. xxiii), so notes are updated between printings, not only between editions. - <1>The story count.</1> Chapter 2 says the directions "are followed by forty-two personal experiences" (p. 29), the fourth edition's number. <2>Experience, Strength and Hope</2> (2003) says the first edition had 29 stories (Dr. Bob's and 28 others), so that sentence can't have read "forty-two" in 1939. Our sources have no first edition to show what it said.
7b26fc78e60b: <0>"Unchanged" or "largely untouched."</0> Bill (1955, printed 1957) and <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) say the main text was unchanged; the Preface (2001) and <2>Experience, Strength and Hope</2> (2003) say "largely" (p. xi). The examples above favour "largely."
dd0f0344df1f: <0>Second-edition stories.</0> The Preface counts three first-edition stories kept intact, including "Bill's Story," which is Chapter 1 (p. xi); <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> says "Only two stories from the first edition were retained intact" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003), perhaps counting only the story section. Its own figures (two intact, three edited, two rewritten, 30 new) add up to 37, as the Preface's do without Bill's story, yet it gives the total as 38 stories (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). <2>Pass It On</2> (1984) counts six carried over besides Bill's and Dr. Bob's, and 30 new (Pass It On, 1984).
06208f838022: <0>Fourth-edition stories.</0> The Preface's figures add up to 24 new stories (p. xii); <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> says 25 new stories and 17 kept from the third edition (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). Both arrive at forty-two. Our sources don't explain either difference of one.
439d9d22bd37: <0>When the fourth edition appeared.</0> The copyright page says first printing October 2001 (p. iv); the fourth-edition foreword says it "came off press in November 2001" (p. xxiii).
6fd4e4d3eb86: Because the program text has hardly changed, a reader of any edition is reading essentially the same 1939 words in Chapters 1 to 11. Whether the page numbers match from edition to edition, our sources can't check; it holds only the fourth edition. The stories are another matter: a story quoted from one edition may not exist in another. That's one reason the stories are read as members' experience rather than program text; see <0>Are the personal stories part of the A.A. program?</0> The stories dropped from the first three editions are collected in <1>Experience, Strength and Hope</1> (2003).
40e20c32f521: On copyright, the <0>A.A. Service Manual</0> (2024–2026 edition) says the first and second editions are in the public domain in the United States only, while the third and fourth remain under copyright (A.A. Service Manual).

7ede665b7981: A business meeting is where a group looks after its own affairs: choosing its trusted servants, handling its money, planning its meetings, and hearing from the people who serve it. P-16 (2018) lists these jobs.
5635b9019cdb: The Long Form doesn't use the phrase "business meeting," but it covers everything such a meeting decides. A group answers only to "its own conscience" in its own affairs (p. 563), its leaders "do not govern" (p. 565), it pays its own way and avoids piling up money (p. 564), and its one purpose is carrying the message to the alcoholic who still suffers (p. 563).
c9a3a6e60f6d: So the Traditions are the guide for a business meeting. P-16 says the same: the spiritual nature of the Fellowship, "embodied in our Traditions and Concepts," gives ample guidance (P-16, 2018, p. 30).
d9b01e048cf2: What the Long Form gives a business meeting to work with (1946)
004daa68c6d0: <0>Whose decision it is.</0> For its group purpose there is but one ultimate authority, "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563). In its own affairs each group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience" (p. 563).
269ddee305f0: <0>When to look beyond the group.</0> If its plans affect neighbouring groups, they should be consulted; and nobody should take action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without conferring with the trustees (p. 563). "On such issues our common welfare is paramount" (p. 563).
4c482a4a2017: <0>The money.</0> The group is supported by its own members' voluntary contributions (p. 564). Large gifts and contributions with strings are unwise, and treasuries that keep growing "beyond prudent reserves" for no stated A.A. purpose are a concern (p. 564).
b31f2f6f1260: <0>The officers.</0> A group needs "the least possible organization," rotating leadership is best, and a small group may elect a secretary, a large one a rotating committee (p. 565). They are servants: "They derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565).
7dded1441a08: <0>What's off the table.</0> Going into business, affiliating with or endorsing anything outside A.A. (p. 564), and taking positions on outside controversial issues (p. 565).
a31d237d17f0: <0>What everything serves.</0> "But one primary purpose — that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (p. 563).
d1eba9f6df9d: Most groups, Bill wrote, didn't even choose leaders; they used rotating committees for their simple affairs, which "have only the authorization to serve, never to command" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38). Each committee "carries out what it believes to be the wishes of its group" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947, p. 38). Committees that tried to discipline members, write detailed rules or judge people's morals achieved nothing lasting (P-17, p. 38).
930e44975623: A small historical note: in 1947 Bill used the phrase "business meetings" for the meetings of a <0>club corporation</0> electing its directors, while "strictly A.A. matters" stayed with the groups (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 21; "Money", 1946, p. 29). See <1>What did Bill W. say about clubs and A.A.?</1>
4e719ae45e08: What P-16 says a business meeting does (2018, dated)
d9717f1297a2: <0>When.</0> Usually monthly or quarterly, called by the chairperson or another officer, before or after a regular meeting (P-16, 2018, p. 30).
f8830b53f655: <0>Who votes.</0> A group may ask that "only home group members participate or vote" (P-16, 2018, p. 30).
e8f08a7cdb0a: <0>What it covers.</0> Electing new officers; scheduling meetings; the treasurer's financial reports; reports from the general service representative and other servants; and "apportioning excess funds" among the local intergroup, GSO, and the area and district (P-16, 2018, p. 30). P-16 also describes business sessions as a place for officers' reports "to discuss group affairs and obtain group guidance" (P-16, 2018, p. 14).
1d04756bc6dd: <0>How.</0> Members get all the relevant facts before a vote; reaching an informed group conscience takes time; and "minority, or dissenting, views" must be heard, since they may even turn the tide (P-16, 2018, p. 30). P-16 describes group conscience as aiming at "substantial unanimity" (P-16, 2018, p. 28), and says its result "rests on more than a 'yes' or 'no' count" (P-16, 2018, p. 29).
392654bb23b5: <0>What it isn't.</0> Some groups tried Robert's Rules of Order and found members too intimidated to speak; the Traditions and Concepts give "ample guidance" (P-16, 2018, p. 30).
d655607e9636: P-16 isn't entirely consistent on how decisions are made. Its introduction says groups "function as a democracy, with all plans for group action approved by the majority voice" (P-16, 2018, p. 10), while its group-conscience section asks for substantial unanimity. See <0>Is group conscience a majority vote?</0>
effb353fe6a0: The Long Form doesn't prescribe a format or an agenda. It settles who decides (the group's own conscience, under God as expressed there), who doesn't (any officer, committee or outside body), what the money is for, and what the group exists to do. A business meeting run on those lines is the Traditions at work in one group.

8371cdc9b28f: What part did Carl Jung play in A.A.'s beginning?
0fa64a53cd9c: The Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung treated an American alcoholic, later identified as Rowland H., in the early 1930s. When the man relapsed, Jung told him that medicine could do no more for him, and that his only hope was a genuine spiritual experience, which in alcoholics like him was rare.
eb328d5035e9: The man joined the Oxford Group and got sober. He helped Ebby T. get sober in 1934, and Ebby brought the message to Bill W. That is the chain Bill later traced back to Jung.
42c3288058e9: The Big Book tells the story in Chapter 2 without naming the patient. Today's text names the doctor as "Dr. Jung"; our sources don't show whether the 1939 printing did.
ab7775288ce1: Our sources show no other part Jung played: no meetings, no membership. In 1961 Bill wrote to thank him, and Jung replied. Jung's reply is the source of the Latin phrase <0>spiritus contra spiritum</0>.
b0912724f527: Chapter 2, <0>There Is a Solution</0>, tells of an American businessman of ability and high character who went to Europe for treatment by "a celebrated physician (the psychiatrist, Dr. Jung)" (p. 26). He left with great confidence and was soon drunk (p. 26). When he went back and asked why, "In the doctor's judgment he was utterly hopeless" (p. 26). Asked whether there was any exception, the doctor said: "Here and there, once in a while, alcoholics have had what are called vital spiritual experiences." (p. 27). He described them as "huge emotional displacements and rearrangements" (p. 27). The man's religious convictions, the doctor told him, did not amount to that experience (p. 27).
9a9d7ad23bdc: The chapter goes on to say the man later had the experience and is free (pp. 26, 28), and that the other members "sought the same escape with all the desperation of drowning men" (p. 28). A footnote, added when the appendices were, points to Appendix II on spiritual experience (p. 27). See <0>What is the "spiritual awakening" in Step 12?</0>
d1dc61b4bda2: The Big Book names neither the patient nor Ebby's connection to him. Today's text names Jung in parentheses; our sources have only the fourth edition, so it can't say whether that parenthesis was in the first printing.
701889dd6a33: How Jung's words reached Bill (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)
fa8a00f21185: In Bill's 1957 account, after his own experience at Towns Hospital he read William James and saw the pattern of deflation at depth: "Dr. Carl Jung had told an Oxford group friend of Ebby's how hopeless his alcoholism was" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), Dr. Silkworth had told Bill the same, and then Ebby, another alcoholic, had brought the message (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Before Bill went to Akron, Silkworth reminded him that the doctor in Zurich had told this alcoholic "his only hope of salvation was a spiritual experience" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
c6f7abc52b5c: At the 1955 convention, the Rev. Sam Shoemaker listed "Dr. Jung's simple declaration that science had no answer" among the strands that went into A.A., along with Dr. Silkworth's help and William James (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
712384e7626a: The name, and the letters (Pass It On, 1984)
606d13b078db: <0>Pass It On</0> names the patient as Rowland H., of a prominent Rhode Island family (Pass It On, 1984). It says he was treated by Jung for about a year, got drunk soon after, and went back, to be told more treatment would be useless; in Jung's opinion only a spiritual awakening could help, and when Rowland said he already believed in God, Jung replied that "belief was not enough" and suggested he join a religious movement (Pass It On, 1984). Rowland joined the Oxford Group, got sober, and in 1934 helped Ebby (Pass It On, 1984). See <1>Who was the old school friend in "Bill's Story" (Ebby)?</1>
27ae28d059fe: In January 1961 Bill wrote to Jung to tell him that this conversation was "the first link in the chain of events that led to the founding of Alcoholics Anonymous" (Pass It On, 1984). Jung answered on January 30, 1961 (Pass It On, 1984). He said he had had to be very careful in what he told Rowland, and explained what he had really thought: "His craving for alcohol was the equivalent on a low level of the spiritual thirst of our being for wholeness" (Pass It On, 1984). He ended with a play on the Latin word for both alcohol and spirit: "Alcohol in Latin is spiritus" (Pass It On, 1984), and so the helpful formula was spirit against spirit (Pass It On, 1984). Bill wrote back in March; Jung died that June (Pass It On, 1984).
c03a5fd5f004: <0>The year of the treatment.</0> The timeline in our later printing of <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> says Jung's help to the alcoholic came in 1930 and was "later seen as" the first step toward A.A. (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill's 1961 letter, as <2>Pass It On</2> quotes it, says the man became Jung's patient about 1931 (Pass It On, 1984). The Big Book gives no year.
8bd28fd8722d: <0>What Jung advised.</0> The Big Book has the doctor say only that vital spiritual experiences sometimes happen and that the man's religious convictions weren't enough (p. 27). <1>Pass It On</1> adds that Jung told him to join a religious movement (Pass It On, 1984), and Bill's 1961 letter says Jung recommended that he "place himself in a religious atmosphere and hope for the best" (Pass It On, 1984).
c9522223b964: <0>"Founder" sayings.</0> Our sources don't support calling Jung a founder or member of A.A. The sources describe one conversation with one patient, which Bill came to see as the first link in a chain (Pass It On, 1984).
